en: Leave them on the stem, do not wash them until you cook, and keep them in a closed box lined with dry kitchen paper — wet leaves blacken within two days. Ohioline's method for fresh herbs also works: stems in an inch of water like a bouquet, loosely bagged, water changed daily, up to a week. Curry leaves lose their aroma fast once they go limp, and a blackened leaf has nothing left to give.

Freezing beats drying for this leaf. Freeze whole sprigs dry in a bag and drop them straight into hot oil from frozen; they will not be crisp but the aroma survives, which it does not in the dried leaf.

Sealed boxes keep to the printed date in a cool dry cupboard. A curry block is flour and spice cooked into hardened fat — palm oil or beef fat — so what limits it is the fat going rancid, not anything microbial. Keep it away from the cooker and out of the sun.

Once the foil is cut, wrap the remaining blocks tightly or seal them in a bag. Ohio State Extension gives opened salad oils 1 to 3 months, which is the same rancidity clock. A white bloom on an old block is usually fat crystallising and is harmless; a crayon-like or paint-like smell means the fat has oxidised and the curry will taste of it.

This is where most people actually lose curry: the made-up pot, not the block. Japanese curry is a thick, low-acid, starchy stew that cools slowly in the middle — divide it into shallow containers, get it cold fast, and eat it within three to four days. Reheat to a full boil, stirring, not just to warm.
Made-up curry freezes well minus the potatoes, which go grainy. Portion it flat in bags.
Thinner-skinned than a round passionfruit, so it dries out faster on the counter.
Bagged in the crisper.
Freeze the pulp; it is normally blended into juice.
Ripen at room temperature until it gives to gentle pressure. Like other Annona fruit it is chilling-sensitive, so do not refrigerate it hard.
Only once soft.

Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture says to cut the leafy tops off first, seal the cut end with cling film, wrap the whole root in paper, bag it and keep it somewhere cool and shaded. The leaves keep pulling water out of the root if you leave them on.
Ohio State gives beets, carrots and radishes 1 to 2 weeks refrigerated, with the leafy tops removed. Grated daikon should be used the same day.

Airtight container in a cool, dry, dark cupboard — Ohioline gives dried beans and legumes 12 months that way, and USU notes that food-grade polyethylene bags run to a year or more. Two things go wrong slowly: light bleaches the colour, and oxygen turns the small amount of oil in the seed. A third goes wrong faster — pantry weevils. Bay leaves are folklore; a genuinely airtight jar is not. Oiled toor dal, sold with a light film of oil to deter insects, should be rinsed in warm water before cooking.
Decant into a sealed jar as soon as the bag is opened.

Dashi is a plain, unsalted, low-acid stock and behaves like any other homemade broth: cool it quickly, get it into a covered container in the fridge at 4 °C or below, and use it within three to four days. It has no salt, sugar or acid barrier at all, which is why it is the shortest-lived thing in this batch.
Freeze in ice-cube trays or flat in bags so you can break off what a dish needs. This is how most Japanese home cooks handle a batch of 一番だし.

Dry granules and sealed sachets keep about a year in a cool dry cupboard. Keep them airtight — the granules are hygroscopic and cake into a solid lump the moment they meet humidity, which is the usual end of a jar of だしの素 in a humid kitchen.

Once you have made it up into liquid stock, it is stock: covered, at 4 °C or below, three to four days. Concentrated liquid dashi in a bottle should be refrigerated after opening and used to the maker's instruction — the printed date stops applying once the bottle is opened.
Unopened tubs keep to the printed date in a cool dark place. Traditional 된장 was kept for years in an earthenware jar outdoors at high salt; supermarket tubs are milder and less forgiving.

Refrigerate after opening, surface pressed flat under its plastic disc or cling film, clean dry spoon only. Darkening and a stronger, more ammoniac aroma over time are normal ageing. A white bloom on the surface is usually yeast and can be stirred in or scraped off; fuzzy coloured mould means discard.

Same two clocks as idli batter, with the quality window running the other way: dosa batter is at its best after it has soured a little, so days two and three are the good ones and day one can taste flat. Past about five days it turns sharply acidic and thins out. Refrigerate at 4 °C or below straight after the rise, keep a clean spoon for it, and discard any batter that smells of alcohol or acetone, has gone pink or grey, or was left out overnight in a warm room — CFS notes that the toxins Bacillus cereus forms in starchy food while it multiplies cannot be destroyed by reheating.
Sealed jars keep on the shelf to the printed date. Store in a cool dark cupboard away from the stove.

Doubanjiang is protected by salt, acidity and fermentation, not by refrigeration. The FDA's labelling guidance lists acidification (pH 4.6 or below), salt and low water activity as barriers that work the same way refrigeration does, and notes that condiments such as mustard, salsa and spaghetti sauce carry a 'refrigerate after opening' line to retard quality loss rather than to prevent illness. A jar left out will darken and lose aroma long before it becomes dangerous.

Refrigerate once opened. Always use a clean dry spoon — a wet spoon introduces water and mould, which is the usual way a jar of 豆瓣醬 is lost. Level the surface and press the paste down so no air pocket sits on top.

Douhua is soy milk set with a coagulant and nothing else — no acid, no salt, no preservative — so it inherits soy milk’s risk profile. The CFS tells shops selling their own soy milk to clear stock within a day of production and consumers to refrigerate it at 4 °C or below immediately. Keep the syrup separate; a bowl already sweetened and topped will not keep.

Not a counter food. Hot douhua may be held above 60 °C; cold douhua must be at 4 °C or below. The gap between the two is where Bacillus cereus grows, and the spores survive the boiling of the soy milk.
Freezing wrecks the curd — it turns spongy and weeps. This is deliberate in 凍豆腐 but ruins douhua.
Sealed, cool, dry and dark. The failure mode is not bacteria but rancidity — these are oily fish, and the give-away is a sharp paint-like smell and a yellow-brown cast on what should be silver.
Better than the cupboard in a warm or humid kitchen. Keep the bag sealed so the fish do not perfume the milk.
The usual Japanese advice for 煮干し once opened: freeze it, and use straight from frozen for dashi.

Cool, dry and dark, in a sealed glass jar. NCHFP: dried vegetables keep about half as long as dried fruit, and dried fruit runs 1 year at 60 °F but only 6 months at 80 °F — so a warm kitchen halves the figure again. Pods should still bend without snapping; brittle, faded, dusty-smelling chiles have lost their aroma even if they are safe.

Sealed in a bag in the freezer, dried pods keep their colour and perfume far longer than in a cupboard, and freezing also settles any insect eggs that came in with them. Bring them to room temperature before opening the bag so they do not pick up condensation.
Mung-bean starch noodles are almost pure dried starch and keep for a long time in a sealed bag in a dry cupboard. Soaked or cooked they become a wet starch food and belong in the fridge.
Reseal; the bundles are hygroscopic and go cloudy and soft in a damp kitchen.
NCHFP gives dried vegetables about 6 months at 60 °F and 3 months at 80 °F; Ohio State gives dried vegetables a year at 70 °F. Airtight and dark — light bleaches the colour out.
Sealed. Soak in cold water and rinse well before cooking, and use the soaked buds the same day.

Dried rice vermicelli is shelf-stable purely because it has been dried; keep it in the sealed bag in a dry, ventilated cupboard away from the stove. Once soaked or cooked it becomes a wet rice product and must be refrigerated.
Reseal tightly — the strands are brittle and hygroscopic, and damp bundles mould from the inside.

Airtight, cool, dry and dark. Conpoy is drier and less oily than dried shrimp, so it keeps longer, but it is expensive enough that most households refrigerate or freeze it anyway. A white bloom of amino-acid crystals is normal; fuzzy grey or green mould is not.
Sealed jar in the fridge is the standard Hong Kong practice for good conpoy.
Freeze the sealed jar; bring it to room temperature before opening so condensation does not settle on the scallops.

Airtight jar in a cool, dry, dark cupboard. Hong Kong's CFS rule for goods that need no refrigeration is a cool dry spot in a sealed or covered container. Check the jar often: dried shrimp that has picked up moisture goes tacky, then musty, then mouldy.
Most Chinese kitchens keep 蝦米 in the fridge rather than the cupboard, and in a humid climate that is the sensible choice — it slows the oil going rancid and keeps pantry moths out.
Double-bag it; the smell transfers to everything else in the freezer.
Same rule as other Japanese dried noodles: 直射日光及び高温多湿を避け保存. Buckwheat flour carries more oil than wheat, so a hot cupboard turns dried soba stale-smelling long before it is unsafe — buy small packs.
Airtight, away from anything aromatic; the federation's guideline specifically warns about smell transfer.

Despite the name, 豆干 is not a dry food — it is pressed, still-moist bean curd and spoils like fresh tofu. Keep it at 4 °C or below, sealed, and use the printed date. Marinated and braised versions go slimy on the surface first; discard at the first sour smell.
Freezes better than fresh tofu because it holds less water. Slice or shred before freezing.

The 全国乾麺協同組合連合会 labelling guideline tells members to print 直射日光及び高温多湿を避け保存 — keep out of direct sun, heat and damp — and to warn on-pack that dried noodles pick up strong smells, so store them away from spices, soap and detergent. Dried noodles carry no preservative; their keeping quality is entirely the low moisture.
Reseal or decant into an airtight jar. At roughly 12% moisture they will mould or attract pantry insects in a humid kitchen.

Store the brittle dry sticks or sheets in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark cupboard. NCHFP puts recommended storage of dried foods generally at 4 months to 1 year, shorter the warmer the room. Any softness, musty smell or visible mould means it has picked up moisture — throw it out.
Freezing in a sealed bag protects the oil-rich sheets from going rancid in a warm kitchen.
Do not refrigerate.

Uncooked pearls are dried cassava starch and keep well sealed in a dry cupboard. They harden and crack with age — old pearls never soften properly no matter how long you boil them, which is a texture failure rather than a safety one.
Reseal tightly; damp pearls fuse into a solid lump and can mould.

A retorted tin or jar bought off an ambient shelf is shelf-stable to its date — that is a commercial sterilisation, not the fat. A crock of home-made confit is not, and this is where the tradition and the modern kitchen part company. Meat submerged under a fat seal is a low-acid food in an anaerobic environment, which is the classic setting for Clostridium botulinum, and NCHFP's rule for foods held under oil at room temperature is that they belong in the refrigerator. The old farmhouse practice relied on a cold stone cellar, a heavy salt cure and a short season; a warm modern kitchen supplies none of those.

An unopened chilled pack keeps to its printed date at or below 4 °C. Home-made confit, salted overnight, cooked slowly in fat, then packed into a sterile jar and covered completely with strained fat with no air pockets, keeps for weeks in the refrigerator — but no agency publishes a number for it, so this record will not invent one. Keep it cold, keep it covered, and use your nose.

Break the fat seal and the clock resets, exactly as with rillettes. What is underneath is a cooked meat dish: 3 to 4 days at or below 4 °C, New Mexico State's figure. Lifting a leg out and smoothing the fat back over the rest restores the look of a seal but not the seal itself — the fat has been broken, contaminated and re-set over a surface that has met a spoon and the air.
New Mexico State gives cooked meat dishes 2 to 3 months frozen. Freeze the legs individually with a good coat of fat on them; the fat is excellent protection against freezer burn.

Unopened, in a cool dark cupboard. The jar or can is commercially heat-processed and shelf-stable; check the date on the lid. A can that is bulging, leaking or rusted through goes in the bin unopened. Homemade dulce de leche is not shelf-stable and belongs in the fridge from the moment it cools.

Once opened, keep it covered at or below 40 °F (4 °C) and always take it out with a clean spoon — a buttery knife is what turns a jar mouldy. It stiffens to a paste when cold; stand the jar in warm water rather than microwaving it. Decant anything left in an opened can into a glass jar.

Fresh wheat dough rounds. Keep the stack sealed and lying flat; once air reaches them the edges dry and will not seal. A dried edge is a quality problem — a slimy or sour-smelling stack is a safety one, so discard it.
Freeze flat in the sleeve. Thaw in the fridge, still wrapped, so condensation does not glue the sheets together.

Keep a whole, uncut fruit at room temperature until it is ripe. Philippine agricultural research recorded pods splitting 8 to 10 days after harvest in ambient tropical conditions, and the fruit is best eaten before it splits.

Refrigerate only once ripe, and only the flesh, sealed in an airtight container so the aroma does not transfer to everything else. Durian is chilling-sensitive: damage appeared within two weeks at 7 °C, so do not hold a whole fruit cold for long.
Freeze the flesh in portions with the seeds removed. This is how durian is traded internationally, and the texture holds up better than most fruit.

Ohio State's unopened hard-cheese figure. Edam is made from part-skim milk, so it has less fat to go rancid than a full-fat cheese and its wax coat is a real barrier — a sealed ball is a long keeper at 0–5 °C.

Ohio State's opened hard-cheese figure. Once you have breached the wax, wrap only the cut face and leave the waxed surface uncovered; sealing the whole thing in plastic traps moisture against the wax and grows mould underneath it where you cannot see it.
Acceptable for cooking use; it comes out drier and more crumbly.
Freezing guidance applies to egg dishes after baking.

Only for what you will use soon. Egusi is roughly half oil, which is why it thickens a stew and also why it turns — rancid egusi is bitter and the smell is unmistakable once you know it. Ground egusi has far more exposed surface than whole seed and goes off several times faster, so grind in small batches.
Airtight, and sealed hard — it takes up fridge smells as readily as any nut.
The right place for a big bag, whole or ground. Use it straight from the freezer.

Leave enoki in its original sealed bag until you use it and keep it cold — chilled, packaged enoki has been linked to listeria outbreaks, so cook it rather than eating it raw. Slimy or brown-tipped clusters go in the bin.
Stand the stems in a little water like cut flowers, or wrap them in a barely damp cloth in a bag. Epazote bruises black where it is crushed, so store the sprigs loose rather than packed.

Freezing turns the leaves black and slack, but the flavour survives and epazote is only ever used cooked — a bag of frozen sprigs dropped into a pot of black beans works. Do not expect to garnish with it.
Benefits from being stored in airtight containers and out of direct light.

Unopened jars keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard. Hong Kong's Centre for Food Safety warns that fermented bean curd has been found contaminated with Bacillus cereus, and advises buying only from reputable suppliers, checking the date, and finishing it within the stated period.

Refrigerate after opening. Always lift cubes out with a clean dry spoon and keep them fully covered by their brine or wine — the salt and alcohol are what hold spoilage off, and a wet or food-soiled spoon seeds the jar. Discard if the brine turns cloudy, gassy or smells of ammonia.

Dry 豆豉 is a salt-cured, part-dried bean: an airtight jar in a cool dark cupboard is all it needs, and the FDA's labelling guidance is the reason why — salt and low water activity (aw 0.85 or below) are preservation barriers in their own right. Do not rinse the beans before storing, only before cooking, and never put a damp spoon in the jar.

In a humid climate the fridge or freezer is the safer cupboard: it stops the beans absorbing moisture, going tacky and then mouldy, and keeps pantry moths out. No agency publishes a cold-storage figure for 豆豉, so none is given. Softer wet-packed 濕豆豉 in oil or brine is a different product — refrigerate that after opening and follow the jar.

Keep the block submerged in its brine at or below 4 °C. Hong Kong's CFS names feta among the soft cheeses to avoid if you are pregnant, elderly or immunocompromised, because soft cheeses are less acidic and hold more moisture — a favourable environment for Listeria monocytogenes, which grows slowly even at 0 °C. Choose feta made from pasteurised milk.
Freezing works only for cooking use — the curd goes crumbly and grainy on thawing. Freeze it drained, not in brine.

Keep the roll sealed and frozen flat. Thaw it slowly — overnight in the fridge, then an hour at room temperature still in its wrapper. Thawing it fast, or refreezing a thawed roll, is what makes the sheets crack and weld together.

Once the roll is opened, rewrap it tightly in plastic and use it up within a few days. Keep the stack you are not working with under a damp tea towel — filo dries into shards in minutes on an open bench.

Japan's tofu-industry HACCP guide, published by MHLW, sets 木綿豆腐 (cotton/firm tofu) at refrigerated 10 °C or below with a use-by of roughly 3 days. Taiwan's 農業部 says loose traditional tofu is best eaten the day it is bought and within two days at the outside. Keep it submerged in clean cold water in a covered box and change the water daily.
Freezing turns the block spongy and chewy — this is deliberate in dishes like 凍豆腐. Drain and press before freezing.

Fish balls look shelf-stable and are not. Japan's food sanitation standards classify them as 魚肉ねり製品 and require storage at 10 °C or below unless the pack has been retorted at 120 °C for 4 minutes or has a pH of 4.6 or less or water activity of 0.94 or less — home fish balls meet none of those. Keep them at 4 °C or below and cook them through.
Japan's standard for frozen fish-paste products is −15 °C or below; a domestic freezer at −18 °C is comfortably inside that. Freeze in a single layer first so they do not fuse into a block.
Cool dark cupboard, capped. Unopened bottles keep for years — fish sauce is anchovy fermented under something like a quarter of its weight in salt.

The 'refrigerate after opening' line on the bottle is about quality, not safety. The FDA's labelling guidance is explicit that salt and low water activity (aw 0.85 or below) are preservation barriers in their own right, and that the condiments carrying this instruction do so 'to retard deterioration in the quality of the food'. An open bottle on the shelf will darken and turn from savoury towards harsh over months; it does not become hazardous. Salt crystals settling out of an old bottle are just salt.

Refrigeration slows the darkening and keeps the aroma cleaner, which is why many Thai and Vietnamese kitchens do it. No agency publishes a timeline for refrigerated fish sauce and none is invented here.
Not necessary.
Nnot necessary.

Airtight, cool and dark. Freekeh is harvested green and fire-roasted, so it arrives already smoky; what you are guarding against is the germ oil turning, which reads as a flat, slightly bitter taste rather than a smell. Cracked freekeh has more cut surface than whole and keeps less well.
Worth doing for a big bag, and it settles any question of weevils.

Japan's HACCP guide for small fresh-noodle makers, issued under MHLW and MAFF, classifies 生めん (raw) and 茹めん (par-boiled) noodles as refrigerated goods that must be held at 10 °C or below, and requires boiled noodles to be chilled to 10 °C within minutes of leaving the water. Treat the printed use-by date as the real limit and keep the pack cold, not in the door.
Once the pack is open the acid dip and modified atmosphere that hold the noodles stop working. Cook them within a day or two.
Freeze in the unopened pack, or portion and bag. Boil straight from frozen.

Buy them and eat them the same day, or refrigerate immediately. Hong Kong's CFS tells consumers to keep perishable foods including fresh 河粉 and 米粉 at 4 °C or below, and Taiwan's 農業部 says wet rice products such as 粄條, 米苔目 and 蘿蔔糕 must be held below 7 °C. Never leave them out on the counter.

The CFS says wet rice-noodle products with a shelf life beyond one day should be kept frozen through transport, storage and sale — especially in warm weather. Freezing at home works but the sheets crumble on thawing; steam them straight from frozen.

MHLW's HACCP model for noodle manufacture works through a real ゆでそば (boiled soba) spec sheet: 保存方法 要冷蔵（10℃以下）, 賞味期限 D+9 — nine days from production, sealed, at 10 °C or below. It is acid-dipped at pH 4.8-5.8 and cooled to below 10 °C within 30 minutes of packing. Your pack's printed date wins over this figure.
Open the pack and the acidity and low oxygen no longer protect it. Cook within a day or two.
Freeze in the sealed pack; buckwheat aroma fades quickly either way.

Hong Kong’s CFS notes that shop-made soy milk has a short shelf life and advises clearing stock within one day of production; consumers should drink it promptly or refrigerate it at once at 4 °C or below. Soy milk is a low-acid, high-protein liquid — Bacillus cereus spores survive the boil and grow if it cools slowly.

The CFS cooling rule for hot soy milk that is going to be served cold: down to 20 °C within 2 hours, then to 4 °C within a further 4 hours or less. Soy milk kept for hot drinking must stay above 60 °C. Anything in between is the growth range — a jug of warm 豆漿 on the counter is a genuine hazard, not a nostalgia.
Freezing splits it. The protein and the water separate and no amount of shaking brings it back; use it in cooking if you have frozen some.

A cool, dark, airy spot — turmeric is a tropical rhizome and, like ginger, is chilling sensitive below about 12 °C (54 °F), so a few days out of the fridge does it no harm. It dehydrates and shrivels quickly in a dry kitchen.

Unpeeled, in a paper bag or a loosely closed box in the crisper. Cold is a compromise: the fridge is well below the 12–14 °C the rhizome actually wants, so expect skin darkening and pitting eventually, but it holds off mould and shrivelling for a couple of weeks. It stains everything it touches, cutting board and fingers included.
Freeze it whole and unpeeled, then grate from frozen — much the easiest way to handle it and no loss of colour.

Boiled udon is a 茹めん under Japan's 生めん類の衛生規範 and must be kept at 10 °C or below; the MHLW fresh-noodle HACCP guide requires it to be cooled to 10 °C promptly after boiling and held there. Go by the printed use-by date.
Sealed packs rely on an acid dip or post-pack pasteurisation. Once opened, cook within a day or two.
Udon freezes unusually well — commercial 冷凍うどん is sold this way. Boil from frozen; do not thaw first or it goes slack.
It is not safe to cook and eat a whole lobster if it is dead at the time of preparation.

Japan's MHLW HACCP guide for fried bean-curd products gives 厚揚げ (thick fried tofu) refrigerated storage at 10 °C or below and a use-by of roughly one week, and stresses that it must be chilled immediately after frying because the inside is still plain tofu.
Freeze in a bag with the air pressed out; the fried skin goes rancid before the tofu goes off.
Keep the bag at -18 °C or below, deep in the freezer rather than in the door, and do not overfill the cabinet — crowding blocks airflow and lets the temperature drift.

Do not thaw dumplings on the counter: the surface climbs into the 7-60 °C danger zone while the middle is still frozen, which the TFDA names as the biggest risk in home thawing. Boil or pan-fry straight from frozen, or thaw in the fridge and cook the same day. Never refreeze thawed raw dumplings.
Thawing in the refrigerator is not recommended.
